title: Naming a value
objectives: Store values in variables with assignment
Update a variable using its own old value
Predict what each name holds after several assignments

screens.prose:
A program can give a value a name and use the name later.

```python
price = 12
print(price * 3)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You read line 2 as text to repeat. `price` has no quotes, so Python looks up the value it holds, 12.

options.text: An error: price is not a number
options.why: You expected Python to forget line 1. Line 1 stored 12 in price, and line 2 uses it.

hints.text: What value does line 1 store in price?
price stands for 12, so `price * 3` is `12 * 3`.

feedback.correct: Python swapped price for 12, then multiplied.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Replace price by the value line 1 gave it.

explain.text: Line 1 stores the value 12 under the name `price`. Line 2 looks the name up, finds 12, and prints `12 * 3`, which is 36. A name that holds a value is called a **variable**.

screens.prose:
Picture each name as a labelled box that holds one value. Python runs these two lines.

```python
price = 12
qty = 3
```

state.caption: Names are boxes. Values are cards.

screens.question: Drag each value into the box that line puts it in.

hints.text: Read each line as: put the value on the right into the box named on the left.
Line 1 is about the box price and the value 12.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line puts the value on its right into the box named on its left.

byKey.c12: Line 1 says `price = 12`, so 12 goes into the price box.
byKey.c3: Line 2 says `qty = 3`, so 3 goes into the qty box.
byKey.c5: No line mentions 5, so it stays in the tray.

explain.text: Each line put the value on its right into the box named on its left. This is called **assignment**, and `=` is the assignment sign. The 5 is in no box, so the program cannot reach it.

screens.prose:
The box qty already holds 3. Then Python runs a second line.

```python
qty = 3
qty = 5
```
screens.question: Show what the box holds after line 2. A box holds one value.

hints.text: Line 2 is an assignment too. What does it put in the box?
Line 2 puts 5 into qty.

feedback.correct: qty holds 5 now, and the 3 is gone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A box holds one value at a time.

byKey.c5: Line 2 puts 5 into the qty box.
byKey.c3: You kept 3 in the box. Line 2 replaces it, so take the 3 out.

explain.text: The second assignment replaced 3 with 5. Nothing holds 3 any more, so Python throws it away. A variable holds one value at a time: the latest one.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.prose: Write the assignments yourself. A name starts with a letter and has no spaces. Use lower case, as in `price`.
screens.question: Make `price` hold 12.5 and `qty` hold 4. Then print `price * qty`.

widget.starter: # Three lines: two assignments, then a print
widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests: what your code prints, then the values of price and qty.

hints.text: Each assignment is the name, then `=`, then the value.
`price = 12.5`, then `qty = 4`, then `print(price * qty)`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the spelling of both names and the value each one holds.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. If its last line says `NameError`, a name is spelt differently in two places.

explain.text: `price * qty` looked up 12.5 and 4 and printed 50.0. It is a float because 12.5 is a float. Python reads names exactly, so `Price` and `price` would be two different names.

screens.prose:
One name can be assigned from another.

```python
a = 7
b = a
```
screens.question: Show what each box holds after line 2.

hints.text: Python first works out the right side. What does the box a hold?
a holds 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Line 2 copies what a holds into b.

byKey.a7: You moved a's own 7 into b. Assignment copies: a keeps its 7 and b gets a 7 of its own.
byKey.b7: Line 2 looks up a, finds 7, and puts a 7 into b.
byKey.c10: No line mentions 10 yet, so it stays in the tray.

explain.text: `b = a` looked up a, found 7, and put a 7 into b. a keeps its own 7. For numbers, assigning one name from another copies the value.

screens.prose:
Same two lines, then a third.

```python
a = 7
b = a
a = 10
```
screens.question: Show what each box holds after line 3.

hints.text: Line 3 names only one box. Which one changes?
Line 3 puts 10 into a, and a's old 7 goes. Nothing tells b to change, so it keeps 7.

feedback.correct: a holds 10 and b still holds 7.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Line 3 changes one box only.

byKey.b7: You changed b along with a. `b = a` copied 7 into b at that moment. It does not tie b to a for ever.
byKey.c10: Line 3 puts 10 into the a box.
byKey.a7: a can hold one value. Take its old 7 out when the 10 goes in.

explain.text: Line 3 replaced the value in a and touched nothing else. b still holds 7, because `b = a` copied the value at that moment. Changing a later never changes b.

screens.prose:
This line looks wrong to anyone who knows algebra.

```python
x = 5
x = x + 1
print(x)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.text: An error, because x cannot equal x + 1
options.why: You read `=` as the equals sign of algebra. In Python it means: work out the right side, then store it in the name on the left.
You expected line 2 to leave x alone. It works out 5 + 1 and puts 6 into x.
You read line 2 as a question: is x equal to x + 1? A comparison uses `==`. A single `=` assigns.

hints.text: Which side of `=` does Python work out first?
x holds 5 before line 2 runs.
The right side is `5 + 1`, which is 6. Then 6 goes into x, replacing the 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the right side first, using the current value of x.

byKey.error: You read `=` as a claim that both sides are equal. In Python it is an instruction: compute the right side, then store it.

explain.text: Python works out `x + 1` with the current x, 5, and gets 6. Then it puts 6 into x, replacing the 5. Read `x = x + 1` as: x becomes x plus 1.

canvas.caption: After line 2: x + 1 is 6, which replaces the 5

screens.prose: A running balance works the same way. You start with £1,000 in cash and buy 3 shares at £120 each.
screens.question: Update `cash` with one assignment that uses its old value, then print it.

widget.starter:
cash = 1000
# Update cash on the next line, then print it
widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests: what your code prints, the final value of cash, and that you printed one line.

hints.text: The new cash is the old cash minus what the shares cost.
`cash = cash - 3 * 120`, then `print(cash)`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The new value of cash is the old value minus 3 times 120.

byKey.test-1: Your program should print 640 on one line. Store the new value in `cash`, then print it.

explain.text: The right side used the old cash, 1000, and took off `3 * 120`, which is 360. Then 640 was stored in cash. This is how a program keeps a running total.

screens.prose: Every assignment you did had two steps. First Python works out the right side, using the values the names hold now. Then it stores the result in the name on the left. $$\texttt{name} = \texttt{expression}$$ A later assignment changes only the name it mentions.
screens.question: In `total = total + fee`, what does Python do first?

options.text: Works out `total + fee` with the old total
Checks whether total equals total + fee
options.why: That would be a comparison, written `==`. A single `=` assigns.
Nothing is emptied first. The old total is needed to work out the right side.

hints.text: Think back to `x = x + 1`.
The right side comes first. Only then is the result stored in the name on the left.

feedback.correct: The right side first, then the result is stored.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall which side Python works out first.

explain.text: The right side is computed with the values the names hold right now. Only then is the result stored in the name on the left. That is why `x = x + 1` is a step forward, not a contradiction.

screens.prose: You hold 25 shares priced at £182.40. Your **position value** is price times quantity. Later the price moves to £185.10.
screens.question: Store the value in `value`. Then update `price`, update `value`, and print `value`.

widget.solution:
price = 182.40
qty = 25
value = price * qty
price = 185.10
value = price * qty
print(value)
widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests: what your code prints, then the final value and price (close to the exact amount is enough).

hints.text: Assigning a new price does not change value by itself. What must you do after it?
After `price = 185.10`, write `value = price * qty` again, then print.

feedback.correct: The position is worth £4,627.50 at the new price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recompute value after the price changes.

byKey.test-1: If you printed 4560.0, value still holds the old position. Assign value again after the price changes.

explain.text: At £182.40 the position was worth £4,560. `value` does not follow `price` on its own: it holds the number worked out when that line ran. Recomputing after the move gives £4,627.50, a gain of £67.50.

ideas: A variable is a name that holds a value. `=` stores the value on the right in the name on the left.
Python works out the right side first, with the current values, then stores the result.
`b = a` gives b the value a has now. A later change to a leaves b where it was.

formula.name: Assignment
formula.note: Read it as: name becomes the value of the expression.

summary.trap: `x = x + 1` is not an equation. It means: x becomes x plus 1.

quiz.prose:
```python
a = 4
b = a
a = a + 1
print(b)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You changed b along with a. `b = a` copied 4 into b, and line 3 changes only a.
Every name here has a value before it is used, so nothing goes wrong.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Line 3 changes only a.

explain.text: Line 2 copied 4 into b. Line 3 changed a to 5 and left b alone. So b is still 4.

options.why: You expected value to follow price. Line 2 worked out 30 once; line 3 does not redo it.
value holds the result of the sum, not the sum itself.

feedback.correct: value was worked out once, as 30.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A variable keeps the value from when its line ran.

explain.text: Line 2 ran when price was 10, so value holds 30. Changing price on line 3 does not rerun line 2. This is the edge case: a stored result goes stale when its inputs change.

quiz.prose:
```python
x = 2
x = x * 3
x = x + 1
print(x)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow x line by line.

byKey.first: You kept the first value. Lines 2 and 3 each give x a new value.
byKey.order: You added before multiplying. Line 2 runs before line 3: 2 times 3 is 6, then 6 plus 1.

explain.text: x starts at 2. Line 2 makes it `2 * 3`, which is 6. Line 3 makes it `6 + 1`, which is 7.
